title: Your Birth Order May Affect Your Health
paragraphs: Are you the oldest child in your family, or were you born second? According to a major new study from the United States, the order in which siblings are born may be linked to the kinds of health problems they are more likely to experience.

The study was carried out by researchers from the University of Chicago and Columbia University and published in the journal Nature Health in August 2026. The researchers analyzed medical records covering about 10 million siblings in the United States over a period of two decades. They examined 569 different categories of disease and found that 150 of them were significantly associated with birth order.

According to the study, firstborn children were more likely to be diagnosed with certain neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions, including autism, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), Tourette syndrome and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). They were also more likely to have conditions related to the immune system and allergies, such as food allergies.

On the other hand, children born second were more likely to experience migraines, shingles and substance use disorders, as well as digestive problems such as gastritis, which is inflammation of the stomach lining.

Some experts have suggested possible explanations. For example, Dr. Marc Siegel, a medical analyst for Fox News, proposed that firstborn children's immune systems may not be exposed to as many germs early in life, which could lead to allergies. He also suggested that firstborns may receive more attention from their parents. However, these are personal theories and were not tested in the study.

The researchers stressed that the findings show correlations rather than direct causes. The data came from health insurance claims, which may reflect differences in how often people see doctors, how conditions are diagnosed and how much attention parents pay to their children, rather than true biological differences. In addition, factors such as the age of the parents and the time between births make the results more complicated.

For these reasons, the researchers described birth order as a modest risk marker across large populations, rather than a reliable way to predict an individual's health. As Siegel put it, the study opens more questions than it answers.
